Lichen sclerosus is the most likely diagnosis given its classic triad of pruritus, pain with intercourse, and potential for scarring/structural changes—especially in postmenopausal or perimenopausal women (though it can occur at any age); it carries high risk of complications if untreated. Provoked vestibulodynia is highly plausible due to the isolated, intercourse-triggered pain and absence of visible lesions (though it typically lacks prominent pruritus—hence slightly lower confidence than lichen sclerosus). Chronic candidiasis remains common and often underdiagnosed; atypical strains or biofilm-associated infection can cause persistent symptoms despite prior antifungal treatment. Lichen planus—particularly the erosive variant—mimics lichen sclerosus but often features Wickham striae, mucosal involvement, or oral lesions; it’s less common but must be ruled out. VIN is lower on the list because pruritus and dyspareunia are less dominant than visible lesions or bleeding—but high-grade VIN can present subtly, especially in immunocompromised or HPV-positive patients, warranting biopsy. Absence of reported discharge, odor, rash, or bleeding reduces likelihood of infectious vaginitis (e.g., trichomoniasis) or obvious malignancy, and absence of systemic symptoms makes autoimmune conditions like pemphigoid less likely."}
